displayQuote: I'd rather be ruled by a competent Turk than an incompetent Christian

meta.title: Who really said "I'd rather be ruled by a competent Turk than an incompetent Christian"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No Luther work contains it. Wikiquote calls it disputed. It shows up uncited in 1986 and 1988 writing about Pat Robertson, not in the 1500s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'd rather be ruled by a competent Turk than an incompetent Christian'?
meta.ogDescription: Pinned on Martin Luther, but absent from his writings. It first turns up uncited in 1980s commentary on Pat Robertson's presidential run.

answer.label: Not Martin Luther — no source in his writings
answer.authorDates: Attached to Luther in print by 1986; origin unknown
answer.sourceLine: No work by Luther contains this line. Wikiquote files it under “Disputed,” and the earliest source it lists is a 1988 book on Pat Robertson that gives no citation. We found it in print two years earlier, in a 1986 Christianity Today column by Charles Colson, which also cites nothing.

source.heading: Where the line actually turns up
source.excerpt: When it comes to whose finger is on the nuclear button, most Americans would agree with Martin Luther’s assertion that he would rather be ruled by a competent Turk than an incompetent Christian.
trail: 1520, the closest real text. In To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, Luther writes: “They say that there is no better temporal government than among the Turks, though they have no canon nor civil law, but only their Koran.” He is reporting other people’s opinion in the middle of an attack on canon law. He is not saying he would prefer Turkish rule. (C. A. Buchheim translation, Fordham sourcebook ↗)

1986. Charles Colson’s open letter to Pat Robertson in Christianity Today credits Luther with saying “he would rather be ruled by a competent Turk than an incompetent Christian.” Colson cites no source. (Christianity Today ↗)

1988. Wikiquote lists the line under “Disputed” and says the earliest source it has found is Hubert Morken’s Pat Robertson — Where He Stands (1988), p. 42, which credits Luther “without citation.” (Wikiquote: Martin Luther ↗)
2014. Writing about the “wise Turk … foolish Christian” version, Justin Taylor of The Gospel Coalition says: “Luther didn’t say this one, and wouldn’t have.” (The Gospel Coalition ↗)
source.excerptNote: Colson credits Luther but gives no source. This column predates the 1988 book that Wikiquote ↗ names as the earliest source it has found. We cannot say whether something older still exists.

sourceLink.text: Charles Colson, “Dear Pat: Winning Isn’t Everything,” Christianity Today (1986)

source.rightsNote: The wording has no known author and cannot be traced to any work by Luther, so we make no claim about its copyright status. The 1986 Christianity Today column we quote above is itself a modern, copyrighted article. The 1520 Luther passage is quoted from C. A. Buchheim’s translation as reprinted in the Harvard Classics (c1910).

author.name: Martin Luther
author.heading: About Martin Luther
author.metaLine: 1483–1546 · German theologian and leader of the Protestant Reformation
author.bio: Martin Luther was the German friar and theologian whose protest against the sale of indulgences in 1517 started the Protestant Reformation. He wrote at length about the Ottoman Turks, and in On War Against the Turk (written 1528, published 1529) he urged Germans to resist the invasion. The quip about a “competent Turk” does not appear in any of his works. It has been pinned on him by later writers.

cite.sourceCitation: Not found in Luther’s writings. misattribution.heading: Why everyone thinks Luther said it
misattribution.intro: The line sounds like Luther’s practical side, and he really did write a great deal about the Turks. That is enough to keep it attached to his name, even though no one has ever produced a source for it.

items.why: This sentence appears nowhere in Luther’s writings. Wikiquote ↗ files it under “Disputed,” and the oldest sources anyone has found, from 1986 and 1988, give no citation. Luther’s actual position, set out in On War Against the Turk, was that Germans should resist the Ottomans in a secular war of self-defense led by the emperor (Wikipedia ↗).

items.who: “I’d rather be ruled by a wise Turk than by a foolish Christian”
items.why: The same line with different adjectives. Justin Taylor includes it in his list of quotes Luther never said, crediting Carl Vehse’s analysis that it is “diametrically opposed” to Luther’s known position (The Gospel Coalition ↗).

items.who: “I would rather be ruled by a wise Turk than a Christian donkey”
items.why: A cruder version, listed as “Attributed” with no source given (WIST Quotations ↗).

“They say that there is no better temporal government than among the Turks” is genuine Luther, from To the Christian Nobility (Buchheim translation ↗). It reports what others say about Turkish law. It does not state a preference to be ruled by a Turk, and nobody has shown that the modern quip grew out of it.

misattribution.truthLine: Origin unknown. The line is attached to Luther in print by 1986 (Colson, Christianity Today ↗), but no source in Luther’s own writings has ever been produced.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: Both of the oldest appearances we could confirm come from American commentary on Pat Robertson’s run for president. Colson’s 1986 column uses Luther to argue that a candidate should be judged on ability, not faith. Wikiquote’s 1988 source is a book about Robertson. In that setting the line served as a handy Reformation-era authority for a modern argument about separating competence from creed.

The real Luther is more complicated. He saw the Ottoman advance partly as God’s punishment of Christendom. Even so, he urged resistance, and he rejected the idea of a crusade: the fight should be secular self-defense, led by the emperor and the princes. He did note that some Germans “actually want the Turk to come and rule.” Nothing in his writings shows that he was one of them.
context.pull: A quip from the 1980s, credited to a man who died in 1546.
